items.text: COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public authorities law, in relation to authorizing the
metropolitan transportation authority and its subsidiaries to fingerprint
applicants for employment and to obtain criminal histories of such applicants
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6712

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public authorities law, in relation to authorizing
the metropolitan transportation authority and its subsidiaries to fing-
erprint applicants for employment and to obtain criminal histories of
such applicants

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure that the MTA and its operating agencies can effectively check
the criminal records of job applicants for bus operators and other safe-
ty sensitive positions.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one adds a new subdivision 19 to section 1266 to the Public
Authorities Law, authorizing the MTA and its operating agencies to
submit to the Division of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) fingerprints
of job applicants in order to obtain state and national criminal history
record information.

Section two provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Pursuant to section 509-C of the Vehicle and Traffic Law (VTL), the MTA
and its operating agencies must review conviction histories of all
applicants for the position of bus operator, and also must conduct back-
ground checks of other applicants for employment. Until recently, New
York City Transit's (NYCT) Human Resources Department fingerprinted most
applicants for employment by NYCT, the Manhattan and Bronx Surface Tran-
sit Operating Authority (MaBSTOA), and MTA Bus.  The prints were then
forwarded to the City's Department of Citywide Administrative Services
(DCAS) and the criminal history records were obtained from the Division
of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) for review.

As of December 2020, DCAS will only accept fingerprints for NYCT appli-
cants. As a result, the MTA and its operating agencies are struggling to
effectively review other job applicants. DCAS is responsible for compet-
itive and non-competitive civil service applications, tests, and certi-
fying lists in New York City. Section 50(4) of the Civil Service Law
expressly provides authority for DCAS to do so. MTA Bus and MaBSTOA are
not part of the civil service system, as is NYCT.

Without access to criminal histories of applicants for MTA Bus and
MaBSTOA bus operator positions, the ability to effectively enforce
section 509-C of the VTL has been severely diminished. The MTA had
proposed to DCJS an agreement allowing the MTA to send these job appli-
cants' fingerprints directly to DCJS. But DCJS stated that state agen-
cies or public authorities must have express statutory authority to
submit fingerprints to DCJS in order to obtain criminal history records.
DCAS has such authority; the MTA and its operating agencies do not.

This legislation will correct this discrepancy by amending the Public
Authorities Law, allowing the MTA and its operating agencies to submit
to DCJS fingerprints of job applicants for safety sensitive positions
for the purposes of obtaining state and national criminal history record
information.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
